title: Fabric Spark Toolkit — nb_lakehouse_maintenance: acts on the health report, dry-run by default (first-party executable Spark/Delta notebook, the acting half of the toolkit's audit-then-act maintenance pair; staged at content/toolkit-source/)
summary: A five-cell, first-party executable PySpark/Delta notebook that reads the latest run of the health-audit notebook's report table and executes only the flagged actions, dispatching each of the audit's four flag codes to a specific Delta maintenance SQL statement, with a DRY_RUN parameter that prints the planned SQL instead of running it. Every action is logged to a separate Delta log table with a status field (PLANNED/OK/FAILED) and linked back to the audit run that triggered it. The knowledge base already holds this toolkit's broader conditional-maintenance philosophy and the underlying VACUUM/Direct-Lake and table-property-vs-session-config guidance from prior sources; the health-audit sibling source in this batch already captures the flag taxonomy and thresholds, so this extraction is narrow: the specific audit-report-to-action dispatch architecture, its dry-run-by-default safety convention, and the post-action self-verification step, none of which were previously captured.
audience: Fabric data engineers designing the acting half of a two-notebook (audit, then maintenance) automated Delta maintenance pipeline that must never run destructive operations without an explicit, loggable, dry-run-overridable decision trail.
why_it_matters: This notebook demonstrates the concrete separation between observation and action that the toolkit's maintenance philosophy calls for elsewhere: a distinct notebook consumes the prior notebook's versioned health report rather than re-deriving health signals itself, maps each flag to exactly one maintenance SQL statement via a lookup dispatch, and defaults to a dry-run mode that must be explicitly overridden (in the pipeline parameter, not the code) before anything destructive runs. It also demonstrates a concrete post-check pattern: re-querying DESCRIBE DETAIL after a COMPACT action to assert the file count actually decreased, rather than trusting that OPTIMIZE succeeded just because it returned without error.
takeaways: Splitting Delta maintenance into two notebooks — one that only reads and writes a versioned health report, and a separate one that reads that report and acts — lets the acting notebook's action set be a pure, auditable function of the report table rather than re-deriving health signals from scratch each run.

A demonstrated flag-to-action dispatch maps each of four flag codes to exactly one Delta maintenance SQL statement: COMPACT and NEVER_OPTIMIZED both map to OPTIMIZE, PURGE_DV maps to REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE), and VACUUM_OVERDUE maps to VACUUM ... RETAIN <hours> HOURS, with the retention hours held as a named parameter documented as never going below the table's time-travel or CDF consumer window.

The stated production convention is DRY_RUN=True by default, flipped only via a pipeline parameter rather than edited in notebook code, so that promoting the notebook to a new environment or table set defaults to printing the planned SQL rather than executing it until a human or pipeline explicitly opts in.

Every planned action is logged to a separate Delta table before or after execution with a status field (PLANNED, OK, or FAILED), the originating audit run_id, the exact SQL text, and elapsed seconds, and a failed action causes the notebook to assert and stop rather than silently continuing past a failed maintenance statement.

A demonstrated post-action verification step re-runs DESCRIBE DETAIL after a COMPACT action and asserts the resulting file count is strictly lower than the pre-action count, rather than treating the absence of an exception from the maintenance SQL as proof the operation had the intended effect.

claims.text: This notebook demonstrates a distinct maintenance-acting stage that consumes a separate audit notebook's versioned health-report table (filtered to the latest run_id and non-OK flags) rather than re-computing health signals itself, then dispatches each flag code to exactly one Delta maintenance statement via a lookup table: COMPACT and NEVER_OPTIMIZED both map to OPTIMIZE, PURGE_DV maps to REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE), and VACUUM_OVERDUE maps to VACUUM ... RETAIN <N> HOURS — separating the read-only observation stage from the stage that performs destructive operations.

This notebook's stated production convention is a DRY_RUN parameter defaulting to True, overridden only via a pipeline/job parameter rather than a code edit, so that printing the planned maintenance SQL is the default behavior and actually executing destructive Delta operations (OPTIMIZE, REORG PURGE, VACUUM) requires an explicit opt-in each run; every planned or executed action is logged to a Delta table with a PLANNED/OK/FAILED status, the triggering audit run_id, the literal SQL text, and elapsed time, and any FAILED entry causes the notebook to assert and stop rather than continuing past it.

After executing an OPTIMIZE action, this notebook re-queries DESCRIBE DETAIL and asserts the resulting file count is strictly lower than the pre-action file count, treating a successful-but-ineffective OPTIMIZE (one that returns without error but does not actually reduce the file count) as a failure condition rather than trusting the absence of an exception as proof the maintenance operation had its intended effect.
